groups.title: Bits
groups.note: These take a number (a double), truncate it toward zero, wrap it into [0, 2^32) and hand back the result as an unsigned 32-bit value, so they compose without a cast. A shift of 32 or more gives 0, except that `sar` of a negative value gives all 32 bits set (4294967295, which `i32` reads as -1). These are the operations a logic gate, an adder or a RISC-V instruction needs.

groups.title: Binary data
groups.note: A file's bytes are an [Int], one element per byte, 0 to 255. The readers take that array and an offset and decode the bytes there, little-endian, as Python's struct with `<` does; an offset past the end, or an element that is not a byte, stops the run. In the browser `read_bytes` reads the files the page attaches to the run.

groups.title: Reductions, products and broadcasting
groups.note: Arithmetic and comparisons between two arrays (not complex ones) broadcast as NumPy's do: the last axes line up, and each pair of lengths is equal or one of them is 1, so `A - mean(A, axis=0)` subtracts the column means and `A * transpose([w])` scales rows. `sum`, `mean`, `var`, `std` along an axis and `trace` add in NumPy's order (pairwise, in blocks of 8192), so they agree with NumPy to the bit; so does `sum(a)` of a whole array. `keepdims=true` keeps the reduced axis with length 1 (NumPy's keepdims).

items.name: sum (ordered)
items.blurb: the sum of every element left to right from 0.0 (row-major), the order of a Fortran or C loop, in every engine; for a port that must match a reference's last digits. `ordered=false` is `sum(a)`. `dot` and `prod` always go left to right and take `ordered=true` to say so

items.name: sum (axis)

items.sig: mean(a) · mean(a, axis=axis) · mean(a, axis=axis, keepdims=keepdims)
items.blurb: NumPy's pairwise sum divided by the count

items.name: var
items.sig: var(a) · std(a) · var(a, axis=axis) · std(a, axis=axis)
items.blurb: population variance (divides by n) and its square root, NumPy's order

items.name: prod

groups.title: Databases (SQLite)
groups.note: SQLite (third_party/sqlite, public domain) is built into viv and compiled beside a C program that uses these (`viv export --with-sqlite`); the browser does not have them yet. A database is a number, its handle. Parameters are `?` in the SQL, bound from a list of strings (as text) or an array of numbers (NaN as NULL), never pasted into it. `db_exec` runs inside a savepoint: SQL that fails changes nothing. A query is one statement giving one column. NULL reads as NaN in `db_col` and is an error in `db_col_int` and `db_col_str` (select COALESCE(x, k)). SQLite's errors are VivError; a misuse (a bad handle, a wrong count of parameters, a NULL in an Int column) is ValueError.

items.name: db_open
items.blurb: open or create the database file; its handle. db_close closes it

items.name: db_exec
items.blurb: run SQL (several statements, or one with `?` parameters) inside a savepoint; the rows it changed

groups.title: Maps
groups.note: A map holds numbers or strings under number keys or string keys (one kind of each per map), in the order the keys were first stored. It is one handle: `b = m`, a def's parameter and a record field all change the same map. See Maps above.

items.blurb: a new empty map

items.name: m[k] = v
items.blurb: store v under k (a key already there keeps its place), or read it; a key that is not there stops the run

items.name: m[s] = v
items.blurb: a string key: printed in its repr, `{'the': 2}`; keys(m) is then a list of strings

items.name: has
items.blurb: true when k is a key of m

items.name: get
items.blurb: m[k] when k is there, else d

items.name: remove
items.blurb: take k out and give its value; without d a key that is not there stops the run

items.name: keys
items.blurb: a new vector of the keys, or the values, in insertion order: loop over a map with `ks = keys(m)` then `for i to len(ks)`

items.name: copy (map)

m[1.0] = 2.0
c = copy(m)
c[3.0] = 4.0

items.blurb: take every key out

items.name: len (map)
items.blurb: the number of keys

groups.title: Group-by on Int keys
groups.note: Written in Viv (lang/viv/std/groupby.viv) and added to a program that calls them, so every engine runs the same code. The keys stay Ints (no float conversion), hashed into an open-addressing table whose slot holds the key beside its group id. A group-by is factorize, then a dense loop: `s[ids[i]] += v[i]`.

items.name: factorize
items.blurb: the distinct Ints of an [Int] column in first-appearance order, and each row's position in them (`uniq[ids[i]] == keys[i]`), as pandas.factorize(sort=False); any Int is a key
items.probe:
keys: [Int] = [30, -1, 30, 7]
u, ids = factorize(keys)
s = int_zeros(len(u))
for i to len(keys) {
    s[ids[i]] += 1
}
show u, ids, s

items.name: factorize2
items.blurb: factorize on two key columns at once: the distinct pairs in first-appearance order, as two columns, and each row's pair id; three columns: factorize2 its ids with the third
items.probe:
a: [Int] = [1, 1, 2, 1]
b: [Int] = [5, 6, 5, 5]
ka, kb, ids = factorize2(a, b)
show ka, kb, ids

items.name: match_rows
items.blurb: a hash join's probe: for each Int of probe, the first row of build with that key, or -1 (pandas.Index.get_indexer)

items.name: key_range
items.blurb: the smallest and largest Int of a column, in one pass (0, 0 for no keys)
items.probe:
ks: [Int] = [5, -2, 9]
lo, hi = key_range(ks)
show lo, hi

items.name: group_sum
items.blurb: per-group sum and row count of an [Int] column in one pass, the groups in first-appearance order as factorize's; keys spanning few values (found inside the call) are slotted by key - lo, others hashed with the sums beside the table; group_sum_num sums a number column
items.probe:
k: [Int] = [4, 2, 4, 9]
v: [Int] = [1, 2, 3, 4]
u, s, c = group_sum(k, v)
show u, s, c

items.name: group_sum2
items.sig: ka, kb, s, c = group_sum2(a, b, v)
items.blurb: group_sum keyed by two [Int] columns: one pass over pair slots when both span few values, else factorize2 and a loop
items.probe:
a: [Int] = [1, 1, 2]
b: [Int] = [5, 6, 5]
v: [Int] = [1, 2, 3]

items.blurb: call a function held in a variable or an array

items.name: release_mode
items.blurb: true under --release, else false, so a program can choose what to run in each mode

items.name: clock
items.blurb: wall time in seconds from a monotonic clock; only the difference of two readings means anything, and only a program with a `#! timing` line may call it (every engine refuses it elsewhere; three-engines lists a timing program and does not compare it)
items.probe:
#! timing
t0 = clock()
t1 = clock()
show t1 >= t0
items.interpErr: error: clock() has no clock to read in the interpreter in a browser; run the program natively or with the direct wasm engine

groups.title: Derivatives and records
groups.note: grad and value_and_grad are reverse mode over a whole def (lang/viv/src/grad.rs): the compiler writes the gradient def before any engine runs, so the three engines run the same generated code.

items.name: grad
items.blurb: the gradient of the number def f returns with respect to its first argument x (a number, an array, or a record of arrays), with the shape of x; the other arguments are constants

items.name: value_and_grad
items.blurb: the value and the gradient in one forward and one backward pass, unpacked on a line of its own

items.name: for_leaves
items.blurb: call def f on each array of one or more records of the same type at once (the records' arrays first, then x), in field order; f may write the arrays in place: an optimizer step over a model

groups.title: Complex scalars
groups.note: The `i` suffix works only on a number, so a loop variable named `i` is still a variable. For arrays of them, see the next group.

items.name: re
items.blurb: real part

items.name: im
items.blurb: imaginary part

groups.title: Complex arrays and the Fourier transform
groups.note: A complex array is packed — interleaved (re, im) doubles, which is exactly how C99 lays out `double complex`, so both engines walk the same memory and agree to the byte. `fft` is radix-2 at a power of two, mixed radix (with dedicated radix-3 and radix-5 butterflies) when the primes of the length are all ≤ 7, and Bluestein everywhere else, so no length is a special case and 2·3·5-smooth ones are fast. The twiddle factors and factorization for each length are computed once and reused. Whole-array arithmetic works on complex arrays: `a + b`, `a * b`, a real array or a real or complex scalar on either side of `*`, `/` by a scalar, and `@`. Convention: `fft` is unscaled with exp(−2πikn/N); `ifft` carries the 1/N — the same as numpy and FFTW.

items.name: czeros
items.blurb: a complex array of zeros, rank 1 to 4

items.name: fft
items.blurb: forward transform, in place, any length
items.probe:
a = czeros(8)
a[0] = 1.0
fft(a)
show re(a[3])

items.name: ifft
items.blurb: inverse transform, in place; ifft(fft(x)) returns x to rounding error
items.probe:
a = czeros(6)
a[1] = 1.0
fft(a)
ifft(a)
show re(a[1])

items.name: re (array)
items.blurb: real parts, as a real array of the same shape

items.name: im (array)
items.blurb: imaginary parts, as a real array

items.name: abs (array)
items.blurb: magnitudes — what you plot as a spectrum

items.name: conj (array)
items.blurb: the conjugate, as another complex array

items.name: complex (arrays)
items.blurb: a complex array from two real ones of the same shape

items.name: fft3
items.blurb: forward transform of a rank-3 complex array along all three axes, in place; all-zero lines are skipped

items.name: ifft3
items.blurb: its inverse, carrying 1/N
items.probe:
a = czeros(3, 3, 3)
a[1, 0, 2] = 1.0
fft3(a)
ifft3(a)
show re(a[1, 0, 2])

items.name: eig_herm
items.blurb: the Hermitian eigenproblem: ascending eigenvalues into w, eigenvectors into the COLUMNS of V. Householder to real tridiagonal, then implicit QL
items.probe:
A = czeros(2, 2)
A[0, 1] = 0.0 - 1.0i
A[1, 0] = 0.0 + 1.0i
w = zeros(2)
V = czeros(2, 2)
eig_herm(A, w, V)
show w[1]

items.name: transpose (complex)
items.blurb: plain transpose, NO conjugation: the adjoint is conj(transpose(A)), spelled out where it is meant
items.probe:
A = czeros(2, 2)
A[0, 1] = 0.0 + 1.0i
B = transpose(A)
show im(B[1, 0])

items.name: slab (complex)
items.blurb: slab, setslab, take and put work on complex arrays too; source and target must both be real or both complex
items.probe:
A = czeros(2, 2)
setslab(A, 1, [1.0 + 1.0i, 2.0])
r = slab(A, 1)
show im(r[0])

groups.title: Randomness
groups.note: Park–Miller MINSTD in pure f64, so the stream is bit-identical between the interpreter and compiled C — a seeded Monte Carlo gives the same answer either way. `#! use lib/random` adds randn, randn_matrix, randint, shuffle, randperm, choice, arange and pi, written in Viv over rand(), each documented as the formula it computes so Python can replay it (tools/random_replay.py); `#! use lib/stats` adds mean and std.

items.name: srand
items.blurb: seed the stream

items.name: rand
items.blurb: uniform on [0, 1)

groups.title: Figures and geometry
groups.note: Each of these prints a structured record on stdout, and the page draws the chart from it. Compiled C prints the same record, so a figure is part of the program's output, not a call into a plotting library.

items.name: plot
items.blurb: a line series; consecutive calls sharing x overlay

items.name: scatter
items.blurb: points

items.name: bars
items.blurb: a bar chart: a histogram's counts at its bin centers. A plot() on the same x afterwards draws a curve over the bars

items.name: plot2d
items.blurb: a rank-2 array as a viridis heatmap with a colorbar

items.name: plot3d
items.blurb: a curve in 3-space, rotatable
items.probe:
figure("t", "x", "y")
x = linspace(0.0, 1.0, 4)
plot3d(x, x, x, "curve")

items.name: quiver
items.blurb: a vector field
items.probe:
figure("t", "x", "y")
x = linspace(0.0, 1.0, 3)
quiver(x, x, x, x, "field")

items.name: scene
items.blurb: open a 3D scene; wire/verts output belongs to it

items.name: wire
items.blurb: a 3D polyline, optionally colormapped by a 4th array
items.probe:
scene("s")
x = linspace(0.0, 1.0, 3)
wire(x, x, x, "beam")

items.name: verts
items.blurb: point markers — joints, atoms, nodes
items.probe:
scene("s")
x = linspace(0.0, 1.0, 3)
verts(x, x, x, "nodes")

items.name: figure
items.sig: figure(title, xlabel, ylabel[, xlo, xhi, ylo, yhi[, style]])
items.blurb: REQUIRED before the first plot. The program sets the axis labels and limits; the page adds none of its own. On a plot2d the window is the picture's physical extent and gives it real axes; style is "contour" (overlay level lines) or "pixels" (no smoothing: the cells are categories or counts)

items.name: xtick
items.blurb: inside a figure: a tick labeled with the text at x (a high-symmetry point, a category). A chart with any xtick shows only those x ticks.
items.probe:
figure("t", "k", "E")
x = linspace(0.0, 1.0, 3)
plot(x, x, "band")
xtick("L", 0.0)
xtick("X", 1.0)

items.name: xscale
items.blurb: a logarithmic x or y axis for the open figure: plot the values, not their logs. Ticks at powers of ten; a value of zero or less is a gap, and the chart says how many it left out. "linear" is the default

items.name: aspect
items.blurb: one unit of x as long on the screen as one unit of y, for an orbit or a shape in a plane: the plot takes the height that makes a circle round, and widens a range only if that height would be too tall or too flat. "auto" is the default
items.probe:
figure("orbit", "x", "y")
aspect("equal")
th = linspace(0.0, 6.0, 13)
plot(cos(th), sin(th), "r = 1")

items.name: fill_between
items.blurb: a band shaded from lo to hi over x: a confidence band, a gap, a tolerance. Grouped like a plot; takes its label's color, so a band labeled like its curve is drawn in the curve's color
items.probe:
figure("t", "x", "y")
x = linspace(0.0, 1.0, 5)
plot(x, x, "mean")
fill_between("mean", x, x - 0.1, x + 0.1)

items.name: rangebars
items.blurb: a capped bar from lo to hi at each x: error bars, spreads, ranges. It takes the ends, not a center and an error, so mean ± err is rangebars("m", x, m - err, m + err) and an asymmetric interval is no harder; the center is a plot or scatter of its own
items.probe:
figure("t", "x", "y")
x = linspace(0.0, 1.0, 5)
scatter(x, x, "m")
rangebars("m", x, x - 0.05, x + 0.1)

items.name: grid
items.blurb: the next rows * cols figures become the panels of one picture, row by row, each drawn as it would be alone. share("x") gives each column one x range and labels it under the lowest panel; share("y") does the same along each row; share("xy") both
items.probe:
grid("a swing", 2, 1)
share("x")
t = linspace(0.0, 1.0, 5)
figure("angle", "", "degrees")
plot(t, 90.0 * t, "angle")
figure("torque", "seconds", "N m")
plot(t, 2.0 * t, "torque")

items.name: yright
items.blurb: the series with that label read against a second, linear y axis on the right, with its own ticks and label: two quantities in different units over one x. The legend marks the entry "(right axis)"
items.probe:
figure("swing", "seconds", "newton meters")
t = linspace(0.0, 1.0, 5)
plot(t, 2.0 * t, "torque")
plot(t, 40.0 * t * t, "energy")
yright("energy", "joules")

items.name: style
items.blurb: how the open figure draws the series with that label: a line (solid, dash, dot, noline), a palette slot (s1 to s6), a marker (circle, ring, square, cross, nomarker) and a width (thin, thick), at most one of each. Any other word is a compile error. With no style, series take the palette in order, solid
items.probe:
figure("t", "x", "y")
x = linspace(0.0, 1.0, 3)
plot(x, x, "exact")
style("exact", "dash s2")

items.name: ytick
items.blurb: inside a figure: a y tick labeled with the text; a chart with any shows only those y ticks
items.probe:
figure("t", "x", "E")
x = linspace(0.0, 1.0, 3)
plot(x, x, "e")
ytick("zero", 0.0)

items.name: origin
items.blurb: heatmap settings for the open figure: row 0 at the bottom instead of the top; a blue-white-red map centered on zero for a signed field

items.name: clim
items.blurb: heatmap color limits (beyond them, the end color), and contour lines at exactly these values

items.name: box
items.blurb: in a figure with the style "diagram": a box by two corners. Style words, at most one of each: a color (s1 to s6, ink, muted), a fill (plain, tint, clear), a line (solid, dash, dot, noline), a width (thin, thick), corners (round, square)

items.name: arrow
items.blurb: in a diagram: a line through the points with a head at the last. Words: a color, a line (solid, dash, dot), a width, head or nohead, straight or curved

items.name: note
items.blurb: in a diagram: text at a point. Words: a color, left, center or right, top, middle or bottom (which part of the text is at the point), small, normal or large (11, 13, 15 units), bold, mono

items.name: checkpoint
items.blurb: save the figures so far as one frame; a sequence of frames plays as an animation

groups.title: Animation
groups.note: An animation is a Viv program. Objects are created hidden and named by a string id; transitions reveal, morph and move them. Each call prints one record, and the page plays the records with a scrubber.

items.name: stage
items.blurb: opens an animation; the window is its coordinate system

items.name: axes
items.blurb: ticks and a grid on the stage

items.name: curve
items.blurb: a named polyline, created hidden. The same id again replaces its data

items.name: dots
items.sig: dots("id", x, y) · dots("id", x, y, r)
items.blurb: named point markers; with a radius, discs of that size in data units (atoms)

items.name: circle
items.blurb: a disc

items.name: rect
items.sig: rect("id", x, y, w, h) · rect("id", x, y, w, h, angle)
items.blurb: a rectangle centered at (x, y), turned by angle radians

items.name: segment
items.blurb: a line between two points: a pole, a rod, a spring

items.name: poly
items.blurb: a filled polygon

items.name: frame
items.blurb: a KEYFRAME: advance the clock; an object set again later moves there over the time between. In a keyframed animation objects are visible from creation

items.name: label
items.blurb: text at a point; $...$ is TeX, with \\ for a backslash

items.name: hline
items.blurb: a dashed reference line across the stage

items.name: draw
items.blurb: a curve is drawn on, start to end; anything else fades in

items.name: fade_in
items.blurb: reveal or hide any object

items.name: morph
items.blurb: move a curve's or dots' points smoothly to new data over the given seconds; the point count may change

items.name: move_to
items.blurb: slide a label

items.name: say
items.blurb: the caption until the next say; a value is appended, which is how a caption reports a computed number

items.name: wait
items.blurb: hold

items.name: together
items.blurb: the transitions between them start at the same time

groups.title: Output and testing
groups.note: A failed assert prints what failed (for assert_near, the two values, their difference and the tolerance), keeps running, and makes the process exit nonzero at the end, so a build can stop on it while you still see every failure in one run.

items.name: print
items.blurb: the bare value

items.name: print
items.blurb: text and values on one line, a space (or sep) between them, as Python's print

items.name: fmt
items.blurb: a print argument: the shortest digits that read back as x, as Python's repr

items.name: fmt
items.blurb: a print argument: 1 to 17 significant digits, as %.17g

items.name: fmt
items.blurb: a print argument: a Python format, [[fill]align][sign][0][width][,][.precision] then e, f, g, d, % (or E, F, G)

items.name: narrate
items.blurb: prints a progress line while the program runs, separate from data output

items.name: text
items.blurb: writes an array of Unicode code points as one line of text (the counterpart of chars)

items.name: assert_allclose
items.blurb: elementwise, over arrays
